source: ACOG - Elevated Blood Pressure in Pregnancy & Up to 6 Weeks Postpartum (urgent care protocol, hosted by Urgent Care Association)

content: A postpartum blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher (systolic 140 to 159, or diastolic 90 to 109) is abnormal and can indicate postpartum preeclampsia, even without symptoms. Elevated pressure can appear for the first time after delivery. With a severe headache, blurred vision, or pain in the upper right abdomen or upper stomach it is treated as an emergency. The ACOG-derived protocol covers pregnancy and up to six weeks after delivery.
app_guidance: Rest quietly for a few minutes and check again. If it is still 140/90 or higher, contact your provider today, even if you feel fine. If you also have a severe headache, blurry vision, or pain in your upper belly, call 911 or go to the ER now.

source: ACOG - Elevated Blood Pressure in Pregnancy & Up to 6 Weeks Postpartum (urgent care protocol, hosted by Urgent Care Association)
section: Elevated Blood Pressure With Severe Symptoms
verification: checked against ACOG-derived protocol

blurry vision and high blood pressure

content: Blood pressure of 140 to 159 systolic or 90 to 109 diastolic together with a severe headache, blurred vision, or pain in the upper right abdomen or upper middle stomach is treated as preeclampsia with severe features and needs immediate emergency care.
app_guidance: Call 911 or go to the nearest ER now. Tell them you recently gave birth.

source: ACOG - Elevated Blood Pressure in Pregnancy & Up to 6 Weeks Postpartum (urgent care protocol); University of Iowa severe hypertension protocol
verification: numbers checked against two protocols; home-recheck wording needs clinician review
content: A blood pressure of 160 systolic or higher, or 110 diastolic or higher, is severe-range and counts as preeclampsia with severe features even with no other symptoms. It is confirmed when it lasts 15 minutes or more. Hospital treatment is meant to start within 30 to 60 minutes to lower the risk of stroke.
app_guidance: Do not wait for symptoms. Check again while you arrange care, and call 911 or go to the ER if it stays this high or you have any warning symptoms. Tell them you recently gave birth.

source: Kansas Perinatal Quality Collaborative - Acute Hypertension in Pregnancy & Postpartum Algorithm (ACOG-based); UT Southwestern
verification: secondary (state quality collaborative); numbers consistent across sources
content: A blood pressure below 140 systolic and below 90 diastolic is not in the elevated postpartum range (about 120/80 is a typical healthy reading). A normal reading does not rule out warning symptoms such as a headache that will not go away, vision changes, or upper belly pain.
app_guidance: That reading is in a healthy range, which is good news. Keep checking, and tell me or your provider if you have a headache that won't go away, vision changes, or belly pain, even when the number looks fine.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs
section: Headache That Will Not Go Away
verification: CDC page text checked. NOTE: CDC lists a persistent or worsening headache as a warning sign by itself, not only with vision changes
content: CDC lists a headache that will not go away or gets worse over time as an urgent maternal warning sign for the year after delivery. It is more concerning if it feels like the worst headache of a person's life, or if there is high blood pressure or swelling elsewhere. With vision changes, a high blood pressure reading, or upper belly pain it is an emergency.
app_guidance: A headache that won't go away or keeps getting worse needs attention. Contact your provider right away, and if you can't reach them, go to the ER or call 911. If you also have vision changes, a high blood pressure reading, or upper belly pain, call 911 now. Say that you recently gave birth.

throwing up and it's not normal
content: CDC's urgent warning signs include changes in vision, extreme swelling of the hands or face, severe belly pain that does not go away, and severe nausea and vomiting that is not like morning sickness. These can point to postpartum preeclampsia. A headache with vision changes, or any of these with high blood pressure, needs emergency care. A single sign on its own still calls for contacting a provider right away.
app_guidance: If you have a headache with vision changes, or any of these signs along with high blood pressure, call 911 or go to the ER now and say you recently gave birth. If you have just one of them, contact your provider right away.

content: A seizure, uncontrollable shaking, or loss of consciousness after giving birth is a life-threatening emergency and can be linked to eclampsia, a complication of high blood pressure.
app_guidance: Call 911 now. If someone is with you, ask them to call for you.

source: CDC Hear Her (warning sign); Baylor Scott & White Health; Ascension patient library

content: Heavy vaginal bleeding after pregnancy is an urgent warning sign. Emergency care is needed for soaking through a pad in an hour or less, passing clots larger than a golf ball, bright red bleeding that suddenly gushes after it had slowed, or dizziness, faintness, weakness, or a racing heartbeat with the bleeding.
app_guidance: Call 911 or go to the ER now and tell them you recently gave birth.

source: Baylor Scott & White Health - Postpartum bleeding: what's normal and what's not
verification: secondary (health system blog); stage timing and 6-week range vary slightly across sources

content: Bleeding after birth (lochia) is normal and usually lasts several weeks, up to about six weeks and sometimes a little longer. It starts bright red with small clots in the first days, then lightens to pink or brown, and may start and stop. Heavy bleeding signs, a foul smell, or fever are not part of normal lochia.
app_guidance: Bleeding for several weeks that gets lighter and changes from red to pink or brown is normal. If you start soaking a pad an hour, pass clots bigger than a golf ball, or notice a bad smell or fever, tell me or call your provider.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs

content: Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast-beating heart are urgent maternal warning signs. Trouble breathing includes struggling to breathe when lying flat (needing pillows to prop up) or being unable to catch a breath so that talking and breathing are both difficult. These can signal a blood clot in the lungs or a heart problem.
app_guidance: Call 911 or go to the ER now and say you recently gave birth. Don't wait to see if it gets better.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs; Ascension patient library

content: Swelling, redness, or pain in a leg (or arm) is an urgent maternal warning sign and can mean a blood clot. Combined with chest pain, trouble breathing, or a racing heartbeat it is an emergency.
app_guidance: Get medical care right away; if you can't reach your provider, go to the ER. If you also have chest pain, trouble breathing, or a racing heart, call 911.

source: CDC Hear Her - Warning Signs poster; Ascension patient library

content: A temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher after delivery is an urgent warning sign and may mean an infection such as a uterine, wound, urinary, or breast infection.
app_guidance: Contact your provider right away, and go to the ER if you can't reach them or feel very unwell. Say you recently gave birth.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs

content: Dizziness or fainting is an urgent maternal warning sign. Fainting, or dizziness with heavy bleeding, chest pain, or trouble breathing, is an emergency.
app_guidance: Contact your provider right away, or go to the ER if you can't reach them. If you faint, or feel dizzy with heavy bleeding, chest pain, or trouble breathing, call 911.

app_guidance: That level of exhaustion is worth checking. Tell me what you can and can't manage today, and contact your provider about it.

source: Texas DSHS Hear Her Texas (CDC campaign materials)

content: It is normal to feel tired and have some pain after giving birth, especially in the first weeks. Escalate only if tiredness is overwhelming, pain is severe or worsening, or a warning sign appears.
app_guidance: Feeling tired and sore in the first weeks is normal. Rest when you can and accept help. Tell me if the tiredness feels overwhelming, the pain gets worse, or you have a fever, heavy bleeding, a bad headache, vision changes, chest pain, or trouble breathing.

source: CDC Hear Her - Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms

app_guidance: You know your body best. If something feels wrong, even if it isn't on a list, contact your provider, and always say you recently gave birth. If you can't reach them, go to the ER or call 911.

source: Providence health system; Ascension patient library (paraphrased)

app_guidance: Some soreness and numbness are normal as you heal. Keep the incision clean and dry, hold a pillow against it when you cough or stand, and avoid lifting anything heavier than your baby. Tell me if the pain gets worse, or you notice redness, discharge, or fever.

app_guidance: Please contact your provider if your incision is getting redder or hotter, draining, smells bad, or opens, or if you have a fever of 100.4 F or higher or chills.

Fever or severe belly pain with any of these is urgent.
app_guidance: Those symptoms are common and treatable but should be checked, so please contact your provider. If you also have a fever or severe belly pain, get care today.

source: CDC - Symptoms of Depression Among Women (paraphrased); JAMA PRAMS 2018 summary
verification: primary page text checked
example_phrases: why do I feel so bad after having my baby
content: About 1 in 8 women with a recent live birth report symptoms of postpartum depression, and state rates range from about 1 in 10 to nearly 1 in 4. It is common and treatable, and most people get better with treatment.
app_guidance: You're not alone. About 1 in 8 new mothers have symptoms of postpartum depression. It's common, it's treatable, and it isn't your fault.

source: CDC - Symptoms of Depression Among Women (paraphrased)

I don't think I'm a good mom
content: Postpartum depression symptoms can include crying more often than usual, feeling angry, feeling distant from the baby, and doubting the ability to care for the baby. A lasting sad, anxious, or empty mood is a core sign.
app_guidance: What you're describing can be postpartum depression, which is common and treatable. If it has lasted more than two weeks, is severe, or is getting in the way of your day, please contact your provider, and I can help you find support.

source: CDC; California Dept. of Public Health; clinical sources (paraphrased)
verification: secondary sources; duration varies from days to about 2 weeks

content: The baby blues are common, with tearfulness, mood swings, irritability, and feeling overwhelmed that start in the first days after birth and usually ease within days to about two weeks. Symptoms lasting longer than two weeks, severe symptoms, or worsening symptoms may be postpartum depression, which is not limited to the first two weeks.
app_guidance: Mood swings and tearfulness in the first couple of weeks are very common and usually ease on their own. Rest and accept help. If it lasts beyond two weeks or gets worse, tell me or your provider.

app_guidance: It sounds like you've been feeling low for a while. I'll check in with you again in a few days. Tell me about your sleep and who is helping you.

source: California Dept. of Public Health; Minnesota Dept. of Health (paraphrased)

content: Postpartum depression and anxiety can start during pregnancy or at any point in the first year after birth and can last for months. Risk is higher with a history of depression or anxiety, limited social support, intimate partner violence, young age, or loss of an infant, but anyone can be affected.
app_guidance: Postpartum depression can start any time in the first year. How long have you been feeling this way? If it's lasting or affecting your day, please contact your provider.

app_guidance: Your score suggests you might be struggling. That's not a diagnosis. I'll check in with you again in a few days, and here are some places to get support if you want them.

app_guidance: Your score suggests you may have postpartum depression. This isn't a diagnosis, but please contact your provider soon. You can also call or text 1-833-852-6262 (1-833-TLC-MAMA) any time for free, confidential support.

content: Any answer above zero on EPDS item 10 (thoughts of self-harm) needs a same-day safety follow-up regardless of total score. Many positive answers reflect fleeting thoughts of escaping problems without intent, and some people misread the item, so ask directly rather than assume intent. If intent is present or unclear, provide 988 and, for immediate danger, 911.
app_guidance: Thank you for telling me. I want to ask directly: are you having thoughts of ending your life or hurting yourself? If you are, or you're not sure, please call or text 988 now. If you're in immediate danger, call 911.

app_guidance: I'm glad you told me. Please call or text 988 right now. If you're in immediate danger, call 911. Please tell someone near you. You don't have to go through this alone.

source: MGH Center for Women's Mental Health; CDC Hear Her (warning sign); Texas DSHS Hear Her toolkit (paraphrased)
section: Intrusive Thoughts About the Baby (Distressing, Unwanted)
verification: secondary (academic medical center). NOTE: CDC lists thoughts of harming yourself or your baby as a warning sign, so do not dismiss. Clinician review needed
example_phrases: I keep picturing something bad happening to my baby
scary thoughts about dropping the baby
I'm afraid I'll hurt my baby but I don't want to
content: Unwanted, upsetting thoughts or images of harm coming to the baby are common after birth, especially with postpartum depression or anxiety. When a person is frightened or disturbed by them and does not want to act on them, they do not indicate danger. CDC still lists thoughts of harming oneself or one's baby as a warning sign to bring to a provider.
app_guidance: Scary thoughts like that are common after birth, and having them doesn't mean you'd act on them or that you're a bad parent. Because they can be a sign of anxiety or depression, please tell your provider soon. I can help you find support.

source: Penn State Health; WBUR clinical interview (paraphrased)

example_phrases: I think the baby would be better off if I ...

content: Thoughts of harming the baby are an emergency when the person wants to act on them, feels no distress about them, has a plan, or also has confusion, hallucinations, paranoia, or delusions. This differs from distressing intrusive thoughts.
app_guidance: If you want to act on these thoughts, aren't bothered by them, or are hearing or seeing things, call 911 or go to the ER now, and ask someone to stay with you and your baby.

source: MGH Center for Women's Mental Health; Penn State Health; HHS Office on Women's Health (paraphrased)

example_phrases: I haven't slept in days and feel amazing
someone is trying to take my baby
content: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. Signs include hallucinations, delusions or paranoia, severe confusion, extreme agitation, racing or manic energy, and very little need for sleep. It usually begins in the first two weeks after birth. A family history of bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis raises risk.
app_guidance: What you're describing needs emergency care. Please call 911 or go to the ER now, and ask a partner or family member to stay with you.

source: HHS Office on Women's Health - Perinatal Mental Health Conditions fact sheet (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (federal fact sheet; partially read); confirm details
example_phrases: my heart is racing and I can't relax
I keep checking the baby over and over
content: Postpartum anxiety can show as constant worry, racing or intrusive thoughts, trouble sleeping even when the baby sleeps, dizziness, or hot flashes. Postpartum OCD involves upsetting repeated thoughts and actions repeated to calm them, and the person usually knows the thoughts are disturbing. Both are common and treatable.
app_guidance: This sounds like it could be postpartum anxiety, which is common and treatable. Please tell your provider. You can also call or text Postpartum Support International at 1-800-944-4773.

source: CDC; Rhode Island Dept. of Health (paraphrased)

can I take medicine while breastfeeding
content: Depression after birth is treatable and most people improve with treatment. Options commonly include talk therapy, medication, or both, chosen with a provider. Many mothers can keep breastfeeding during treatment, but medication choices should be made with a provider, who can check resources such as LactMed.
app_guidance: Postpartum depression is treatable, and most people get better. Therapy, medicine, or both can help, and your provider can help you choose. I can't recommend or change any medicine.

source: HRSA National Maternal Mental Health Hotline; Postpartum Support International; 988 Lifeline

It is not an emergency line. Postpartum Support International's helpline is 1-800-944-4773 (call or text HELP). For suicidal crisis call or text 988; for immediate danger call 911.
app_guidance: You can call or text 1-833-852-6262 (1-833-TLC-MAMA) any time for free, confidential support, or Postpartum Support International at 1-800-944-4773. If you're in crisis, call or text 988, or call 911 if you're in immediate danger.

source: California Dept. of Public Health; Minnesota Dept. of Health (paraphrased)
verification: secondary (state health departments)
example_phrases: I don't want anyone to think I'm failing
content: Postpartum depression and anxiety are not a person's fault and not a sign of weakness or poor parenting. Asking for help benefits both parent and baby. Practical supports include childcare help to allow rest, protecting sleep where possible, and telling a provider how things have been.
app_guidance: This is not your fault, and it doesn't mean you're a bad parent. Asking for help is a good step for you and your baby. Is there someone who could watch the baby so you can rest? Tell your provider how you've been feeling.

source: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health - Relaxation Techniques
verification: primary page text checked 2026-10-17 (paraphrased); needs clinician review
example_phrases: I feel stressed, what can I do
content: Relaxation techniques bring on the body's relaxation response: slower breathing, lower blood pressure and a slower heart rate, the opposite of the stress response. Options include slow, deep (diaphragmatic) breathing; progressive muscle relaxation, tensing and then releasing one muscle group at a time; guided imagery, picturing a calm place or scene; and practices such as meditation, yoga and tai chi. They are generally considered safe for healthy people.
app_guidance: Here is one to try now, from the NIH: breathe in slowly through your nose so your belly rises, then breathe out even more slowly, for a few minutes. You can also tense one group of muscles, like your shoulders, for a few seconds and then let go, working down your body, or picture a calm place in detail. If stress or worry is with you most days, tell your care team, because support and treatment help.

source: NIMH - Perinatal Depression; ACOG - Postpartum Depression FAQ
verification: primary page text checked 2026-10-17 (paraphrased); needs clinician review; medication details are information only, never advice
example_phrases: what is the treatment for postpartum depression
can I take antidepressants while breastfeeding
content: With treatment, most women with perinatal depression feel better (NIMH). Treatment usually means talk therapy, medication, or both. Evidence-based therapies include cognitive behavioral therapy (changing unhelpful thoughts and behaviours) and interpersonal therapy (relationships and support). ACOG notes antidepressants may take 3 to 4 weeks to help and pass into breast milk at generally very low levels, and that zuranolone, taken by mouth for 14 days, is the first FDA-approved pill for postpartum depression in adults. A provider helps choose the right option, including around breastfeeding.
app_guidance: Postpartum depression is treatable, and with treatment most people feel better. The usual options are talk therapy, such as cognitive behavioural or interpersonal therapy, medicine, or both. ACOG says some medicines take a few weeks to work, and there is also a newer 14-day pill approved for postpartum depression. Your doctor or midwife can go through which fits you, including if you're breastfeeding. I can't recommend or change any medicine.

source: Postpartum Support International - Get Help

verification: primary page text checked 2026-10-17 (paraphrased); needs clinician review

app_guidance: You don't have to do this alone. Postpartum Support International has free online support groups with other parents, a directory of therapists who specialise in the year after birth, and local volunteers who can connect you with help. You can reach them at 1-800-944-4773 or postpartum.net.

source: ACOG - Exercise After Pregnancy FAQ
verification: primary page text checked 2026-10-17 (paraphrased); needs clinician review
example_phrases: can I go for a walk
content: After a healthy pregnancy and vaginal birth it is usually safe to start exercising a few days after birth, or when you feel ready; after a cesarean birth or complications, ask your ob-gyn first. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, for example three 10-minute walks a day, plus muscle-strengthening on 2 days. Kegel exercises tone the pelvic floor. Exercise can boost energy, improve sleep, relieve stress and may help prevent postpartum depression. Stop if you feel pain.
app_guidance: ACOG says that after an uncomplicated vaginal birth you can usually start gentle exercise like walking within a few days, when you feel ready. After a C-section, check with your doctor first. Build up to about 150 minutes a week, even 10-minute walks count, and stop if anything hurts.

source: ACOG - Breastfeeding Your Baby FAQ
section: Latching and How Often to Feed
verification: primary page text checked 2026-10-17 (paraphrased); needs clinician review
example_phrases: how do I get my baby to latch
how many times a day should baby feed
is my baby getting enough breast milk
content: To latch, cup the breast, stroke the baby's lower lip with the nipple, wait for a wide open mouth, then bring the baby to the breast aiming the nipple at the roof of the mouth. If it hurts or the mouth is not wide open, break the suction with a clean finger and try again. Early hunger cues are alertness, bent arms, fists and fingers to the mouth; crying is a late sign. In the first weeks most babies feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. The more milk is removed, the more milk you make.
app_guidance: In the first weeks most babies feed 8 to 12 times a day, about every 2 to 3 hours, and it's best to offer the breast when your baby brings fingers to the mouth, before crying. If a feed hurts, ACOG suggests gently breaking the suction with a clean finger and re-latching with your baby's mouth wide open. If pain keeps going or you're worried about milk, a lactation consultant or your care team can help.

source: ACOG - Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy FAQ
verification: primary page text checked 2026-10-17 (paraphrased); needs clinician review
example_phrases: how is high blood pressure treated after birth
do I need blood pressure medicine
how often should I check my blood pressure
why is my blood pressure high after delivery
content: Blood pressure often goes up in the weeks after childbirth. People with high blood pressure in pregnancy are usually asked to check their blood pressure at home for 1 to 2 weeks after delivery, and may need to restart blood pressure medication or have the dose adjusted by their ob-gyn. Readings of 140/90 or higher, or symptoms such as a bad headache or vision changes, need a call to the provider.
app_guidance: Blood pressure often rises in the first weeks after birth, so ACOG advises checking it at home if you had high blood pressure in pregnancy. Treatment, like starting or adjusting medicine, is decided by your doctor, so share your readings with them. If you see 140 over 90 or higher, or get a bad headache or vision changes, call your provider now.

source: ACOG - Postpartum Birth Control FAQ

when should I start birth control
content: Ovulation can return within a few weeks of birth if not breastfeeding, and usually by about 6 months if breastfeeding, so pregnancy is possible before the first period. All birth control methods are safe while breastfeeding, though a few are not recommended in the first weeks because of a very small risk to milk supply. IUDs can be placed right after a vaginal or cesarean birth or at the postpartum visit. Experts recommend waiting 18 months after giving birth before getting pregnant again.
app_guidance: You can get pregnant again before your period returns, sometimes within a few weeks of birth. ACOG says all birth control methods are safe while breastfeeding, though a few are best avoided in the first weeks, and an IUD can even be placed right after birth. Experts suggest waiting 18 months before the next pregnancy; your provider can help you pick a method.
